extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, especially those studying Locke and early modern epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains John Locke's claims about the mind's early faculties (perception, retention/memory, discerning, compounding, abstraction) and how they function in forming knowledge. The text is an excerpt from Essay Concerning Human Understanding focused on simple ideas and mental operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight-based judgements may be mistaken for direct perception
rubrics_metrics.description: This judgement apt to be mistaken for direct perception — especially in ideas received by sight, because sight conveys ideas of light, colours, space, figure, and motion which lead us by habit to judge one by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: sight is the most comprehensive sense and its variety of ideas causes us, by use and habit, to take judgments formed from sight for immediate sensation. Example: a man may not notice the bare sensations (characters or sounds) but rather the ideas they excite; many people need reasoning to be convinced of a correct answer to a visual puzzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit unconsciously converts sensation into judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: How, by Habit, ideas of Sensation are unconsciously changed into ideas of Judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: mental operations are very quick and by custom/sustained practice sensations can trigger judgments without conscious notice. Examples/anti-patterns: people cover their eyes without noticing darkness; those with habitual by-words pronounce sounds they themselves do not hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception distinguishes animals from vegetables
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is that which puts the distinction betwixt the animal kingdom and the inferior parts of nature; motions in plants are mere mechanism without sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: treat plant motions (sensitive plants, changes by moisture) as mechanical rather than as evidence of sensation; use difference of mechanism vs sensation to demarcate animals from non-sentient beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception exists in degrees across animals and is adapted to condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception, in some degree, is in all sorts of animals; in some the avenues for reception of sensations are few and obscure, fitted to the creature's state and condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: oysters or cockles likely have fewer or duller senses suited to their immobile life; quickness or variety of sensation is adapted to the needs and capacities of each species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception can decay in old age or disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Decrepit old age or disease may blot out memory and destroy sight, hearing, smell, and taste so that impressions are scarcely perceived or retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: intellectual faculties and retention depend on bodily constitution; long-term deprivation or illness may reduce a person's ideas to the level of lower animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is the inlet of all materials of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception then being the FIRST step and degree towards knowledge, and the inlet of all the materials of it; fewer senses and duller impressions place creatures further from knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: treat perception (external/internal sensation) as the foundational criterion for epistemic material — if perception is absent or poor, the store of knowledge is correspondingly limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention comprises contemplation and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: RETENTION, or the keeping of those simple ideas which from sensation or reflection it hath received, is done two ways: CONTEMPLATION (keeping an idea actually in view) and MEMORY (the power to revive ideas after they have disappeared).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this binary when analyzing mental retention: one immediate (contemplation) and one dispositional (memory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory is the revival of impressions with awareness of prior occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory is as it were the storehouse of our ideas; the mind has a power to revive perceptions which it has once had, with the additional perception annexed to them, that IT HAS HAD THEM BEFORE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that ideas are not literally stored but are revivable perceptions accompanied by a sense of past occurrence; memory differs from current perception by this added sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention, repetition, pleasure and pain fix ideas in memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention and repetition help much to the fixing any ideas in the memory. But those which naturally at first make the deepest and most lasting impressions are those which are accompanied with pleasure or pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: use focused attention, repetition, and emotional salience (pleasure/pain) to make impressions durable; evolutionary rationale: pain/pleasure help avoid harm or seek advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas fade unless repeated; causes of oblivion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas produced by single impressions, or by impressions little noticed, often quickly fade and sometimes vanish quite; if not repeated or renewed, the print wears out and disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: those who lose sight very young forget colours; fevers/diseases can 'calcine' images to dust. Anti-pattern: assuming early impressions persist without refreshment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequently refreshed and multi-modal ideas are most enduring
rubrics_metrics.description: Those ideas that are oftenest refreshed, and those conveyed by more ways than one, fix themselves best in the memory and remain clearest and longest there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ideas of solidity, extension, figure, motion, heat/cold, existence, duration, number — because they recur and are conveyed frequently, they are seldom lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory can be actively searched and emotions can trigger recall
rubrics_metrics.description: In remembering the mind is oftentimes more than barely passive; the mind sets itself on work in search of some hidden idea, and turbulent passions often rouse dormant ideas into view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: memory retrieval can be intentional (search) or spontaneous (emotion-driven); remembered ideas are recognized as formerly imprinted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two memory defects: oblivion and slowness (retrieval failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory may either lose the idea quite (oblivion) or move slowly and retrieve ideas not quick enough for use (slowness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: both complete loss and slow retrieval impede knowledge and practical reasoning; slowness is likened to stupidity when it prevents use of ideas in occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animals (brutes) have memory and use it to imitate
rubrics_metrics.description: This faculty of laying up and retaining the ideas that are brought into the mind several other animals seem to have to a great degree; birds learning of tunes and imitating them shows retained ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument-level guidance: Locke rejects purely mechanical explanations for imitation and maintains animals retain ideas as patterns for later imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment (distinct perception) is necessary for knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: No knowledge without Discernment. Unless the mind had a distinct perception of different objects and their qualities, it would be capable of very little knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: emphasize distinctness and determination of ideas as prerequisites for evidence and certainty; many supposed innate truths rest on clear distinguishing of ideas rather than innate impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit assembles ideas; judgment separates and discriminates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Difference of Wit and Judgment: Wit lies in assemblage and quick putting together of ideas to make pleasant pictures; Judgment lies in carefully separating ideas so as to avoid being misled by similitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: favor careful distinction for sound reasoning; wit's rapid associative operations favor metaphor and entertainment but may not ensure truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and determinateness prevent confusion of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: To the well distinguishing our ideas, it chiefly contributes that they be CLEAR and DETERMINATE; clear ideas prevent confusion even if the same object yields different sensations at different times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a feverish person may taste sugar as bitter but the ideas of bitter and sweet remain distinct if each is clear; ensure concepts are defined clearly to avoid conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing is an operation producing relational ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The COMPARING of ideas one with another in respect of extent, degrees, time, place, or other circumstances is an operation of the mind and is that upon which depends all that large tribe of ideas comprehended under RELATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: relational notions arise from active comparison; use comparison across dimensions (extent, time, place) to form relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounding (composition/enlarging) forms complex ideas from simple ones
rubrics_metrics.description: COMPOSITION whereby the mind puts together several simple ideas and combines them into complex ones; ENLARGING is putting several similar ideas together (e.g., units into a dozen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: forming numeric complexes (dozen, furlong) or compound concepts; composition is a basic creative operation of the understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children acquire naming/signs to express ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When children have got ideas fixed in their memories, they begin by degrees to learn the use of signs (words) to signify their ideas to others, sometimes borrowing words or coining new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical: language acquisition follows stabilization of ideas; naming enables shared reference and categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction forms general ideas from particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: ABSTRACTION is making particular ideas become general representatives of all of the same kind by considering appearances separate from time, place, or other concomitant ideas (e.g., forming 'whiteness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: abstraction yields universals and general names applicable wherever the abstracted appearance is found; crucial for concept-formation and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutes lack the power of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutes do not abstract; they have no use of general signs for universal ideas and so are discriminated from man by the lack of general ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument/explanation: although some animals can utter sounds or signs, they do not apply them as general words; absence of abstraction is a key qualitative divide between humans and animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiots vs madmen: absence of faculties vs mis-assembled ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Idiots lack quickness, activity, and motion in intellectual faculties and so have few propositions; madmen have not lost reasoning but join ideas wrongly and reason correctly from false premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: diagnosing cognitive defect should distinguish between inability to form propositions and erroneous but structured reasoning from bad premises; madness often involves coherent (if false) inferences from distorted fancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological order: explain faculties via simple ideas and appeal to experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The explication of faculties is given after simple ideas for reasons: faculties operate first on simple ideas; simple ideas are clearer; and these operations are themselves ideas derived from reflection. The author appeals to experience and observation as the best way to truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: when analyzing cognitive operations, begin with simplest sensory-derived ideas and proceed to complex ones; prioritize empirical observation over speculative innate-principle claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding likened to a dark room: sensations are the only windows of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: External and internal sensation are the only passages I can find of knowledge to the understanding; these alone are the windows by which light is let into this DARK ROOM (the understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor guidance: treat the mind as initially empty and dark; only sensory and reflective inputs illuminate it. Anti-pattern: positing innate ideas as pre-existing light without empirical warrant.
